title: Updates, patches, and end-of-life devices
body_md:
## An update closes a known path, if it actually installs

Security patches fix flaws that a remote page, document, app or local attacker may exploit. Updating does not prevent social engineering or guarantee that every flaw is known, but running an old vulnerable version leaves a fixable path open. Enable automatic updates for the operating system, browser, apps and router firmware where supported. Then verify they actually finish: a device may need storage, power, Wi-Fi or a restart. An “auto update on” toggle is not proof the last patch installed. Use the OS update screen or the vendor's official app; do not install an update package from an unexpected message.

Before a major update, make a backup and know how to recover important data. For urgent security fixes, follow vendor advice promptly; for feature upgrades that may affect work software, check compatibility and schedule a short maintenance window. Avoid a universal “exactly seven days” promise: urgency and rollout timing differ. If a trusted app says it needs an OS version newer than your device supports, check the device maker's support page rather than downloading a “compatibility patch” from a third party.

## Support is a property of an exact product

End of support means the vendor no longer supplies ordinary security fixes for that product/version. The device can still turn on and run apps; that does not make it suitable for primary email, banking or a password manager. Some vendors release limited exceptional fixes or offer an extended-update program, so check the exact model, edition and enrollment. For example, ordinary Windows 10 support ended 14 October 2025; Microsoft's consumer Extended Security Updates is a separate, temporary path for eligible enrolled devices. A PC merely displaying Windows 10 is not proof it receives ESU. For Windows 10 version 22H2, Microsoft says its KB5126256 licensing preparation package is a prerequisite, not enrollment or a security update; consumers and organizations follow their applicable enrollment routes and exact edition rules. Apple and Android support also vary by model; avoid rules such as “all iPhones older than five years are unsupported.”

For an unsupported device, prioritize moving sensitive tasks to a supported replacement or upgrade. If immediate replacement is impossible, reduce exposure: remove high-value accounts, avoid untrusted downloads, disable unused network services and isolate an IoT device on a guest network where the router actually separates clients. Segmentation limits some lateral movement; it cannot patch the device, protect its cloud account or guarantee containment. A camera or router with no firmware updates is especially worth inventorying because it may stay online unnoticed. Factory reset does not create new security support. Plan disposal or offline use after data migration, and confirm backups before wiping anything.

widget_config.goal: Check whether a device is actually receiving security fixes, install a pending update safely, and make a practical plan for unsupported equipment.
widget_config.today_action: On one phone or laptop, open the built-in update screen, check the installed version and pending restart, confirm a recent backup, and schedule the next available security update. Record one old device whose support status you must verify.
widget_config.scope: General device advice checked 2026-10-20. Vendor support differs by exact model, OS edition and ESU enrollment. Microsoft Windows 10 dates cited only for applicable consumer editions; NCSC documents are UK organization-oriented.

blocks.title: A camera that still streams
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a home camera still works, but its maker lists the exact model as unsupported and offers no firmware updates. It shares a network with family laptops.
blocks.analysis: The picture quality does not answer the patch question. The family plans a supported replacement, removes unnecessary remote access and checks whether a guest network actually separates clients until migration. Isolation reduces some risk but does not secure the camera itself.

blocks.title: A deferred update for a valid reason
blocks.situation: Synthetic: a clinic laptop has a vendor-certified medical app; an OS feature upgrade is offered during a shift, while a security patch and backup are pending.
blocks.analysis: The staff does not click an unknown update link or interrupt care. They verify the update in system settings, back up data, apply the security fix promptly in an approved window and coordinate the feature upgrade with the app vendor and administrator. A short managed delay is not the same as indefinite neglect.

blocks.title: Plan a household patch cycle
blocks.setup: Synthetic exercise: one laptop, one phone and an old camera need different decisions; no real update is installed here.

steps.prompt: The phone says auto updates are on, but the last security patch is old.

choices.text: Check storage, power, Wi-Fi and pending restart in official settings.
choices.consequence: You find why an enabled setting did not finish the update.
choices.explanation: Verify installed state, not just the toggle.
Automatic processes can fail or wait for conditions.

steps.prompt: A message offers a “critical browser patch” as an attached installer.

choices.text: Run the attachment because it says critical.
choices.consequence: The file could be unrelated malware.
choices.explanation: Urgency text does not authenticate a package.

choices.text: Update through the browser or OS official channel.
choices.explanation: The genuine update path is built into the product.

steps.prompt: The camera’s exact model is unsupported. What is the long-term answer?

choices.text: Replace it with a supported model and migrate configuration safely.
choices.consequence: The online device can again receive fixes.
choices.explanation: Isolation is temporary risk reduction, not a patch.

choices.text: Factory reset it every month forever.
choices.consequence: Known flaws still have no fix.
choices.explanation: Reset does not extend vendor support.

steps.prompt: A Windows 10 version 22H2 laptop claims ESU coverage. How do you assess it?

choices.text: Assume every Windows 10 device is covered.
choices.explanation: Eligibility and enrollment are separate facts.

choices.text: Verify exact edition, eligibility, enrollment and recent installed updates in Microsoft/Windows settings.
choices.consequence: Coverage is established by actual enrollment and update state.
choices.explanation: An ESU option or preparation package alone is not enrollment.

blocks.debrief: Replay by separating an available update, an installed update, vendor support and a temporary mitigation for an unsupported device.

questions.prompt: Auto update is enabled but the device has not restarted in weeks. What should you check?

choices.text: Pending restart and installed patch version in system settings.
choices.explanation: Some patches wait for completion conditions.

choices.text: Nothing; the setting proves all patches are installed.
choices.explanation: Enabled is not the same as completed.

questions.prompt: What does a working unsupported device imply?

choices.text: It is safe for all sensitive accounts.
choices.explanation: Working software can retain known flaws.

choices.text: It may function while missing ordinary security fixes.

questions.prompt: A guest network isolates an old camera. What remains?

choices.text: The camera itself and its cloud account can still be exposed.
choices.explanation: Segmentation limits some local paths, not the device’s own flaws.
Network separation is only one layer.

questions.prompt: A Windows 10 version 22H2 PC shows the KB5126256 ESU preparation update. Is it necessarily enrolled?

choices.text: Yes; the preparation package grants coverage.
No; verify actual enrollment and received security updates.
choices.explanation: Microsoft distinguishes a prerequisite from ESU enrollment.
